title: Quick Sort
description: Implement quick sort with in-place partitioning, and understand pivot choice and the O(n²) worst case.

data.text: Sort an array of integers in ascending order using quick sort. It must sort in place, and you should be able to explain when it degrades to O(n²).

Everything hinges on partitioning: choose a pivot value and rearrange the range so that all elements smaller than the pivot come first, then the pivot, then everything larger. Once the pivot is in its final position, recurse on the two sides.

data.title: Lomuto partition (simple, easy to prove)
data.content: One pointer scans, the other marks the boundary of the smaller region.

data.text: The naive 'last element as pivot' choice is O(n²) on already-sorted input, which is a realistic input. Choosing a random pivot first makes that worst case astronomically unlikely while keeping the same code.

data.title: Quick sort O(n log n) average
data.content: Randomised pivot avoids the sorted-input trap.

data.title: Quick sort is not stable
data.text: Partitioning swaps elements across arbitrary distances, so equal elements can change relative order. If stability matters, use merge sort. This is a very common interview follow-up.

data.title: Three-way partition handles many duplicates
data.text: If the array has many equal keys, Lomuto partition degenerates because all equal elements land on one side. A three-way partition (less / equal / greater, as in the Dutch national flag problem) puts all equal keys in their final positions at once and often beats the two-way version on real data.

data.caption: Each partition places one pivot in its final position and splits the remaining work into two smaller ranges.

data.title: Complete solution
data.content: In production .NET code you would call `Array.Sort`, which is an introsort: quick sort that switches to heap sort when recursion gets too deep and to insertion sort on small ranges. Knowing *why* those three are combined is what interviews are testing.
